content_preview.title: Supreme Court Overrules Humphrey's Executor in Trump v. Slaughter, Ending FTC Commissioners' For-Cause Protection
content_preview.summary: The 6-3 ruling lets presidents fire FTC commissioners at will, reshaping the agency that leads U.S. privacy and AI enforcement.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The U.S. Supreme Court on June 29, 2026, ruled 6-3 that the President can remove commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission at will, overturning the 1935 precedent that had shielded the heads of independent agencies from being fired without cause, according to [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-trump-ftc-slaughter-humphreys-executor/). The decision in *Trump v. Slaughter*, docketed as No. 25-332, upholds President Trump's removal of FTC Commissioner Rebecca Sla...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured Analysis using the house Overview / What We Know / Why It Matters for Tech / What We Don't Know framework. At 777 words it sits within the Analysis range. The piece reports a politically charged Supreme Court ruling with precision: the holding, the 6-3 vote, the overruled precedent, the majority's reasoning, and the dissent's objection are each stated and sourced. The tech-relevance section is grounded in the FTC's actual enforcement remit rather than speculation.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 3 sources are on the allowlist (scotusblog.com, cbsnews.com, iapp.org) and all three snapshots fetched successfully with HTTP 200. I decompressed and read each from disk. source-0.html.gz (SCOTUSblog): CONFIRMS the June 29 2026 date, docket No. 25-332, the 6-3 vote, Roberts as majority author, Sotomayor's dissent joined by Kagan and Jackson, and every quote attributed to it verbatim — 'tethered to a highly circumscribed and almost fictional view,' 'unquestionably exercises executive power,' 'removed from the Federal Trade Commission, effective immediately,' 'inconsistent with my Administration's priorities,' 'distorts the structure of Government to fit the majority's theory of unitary, total executive control,' 'distinct historical tradition of the First and Second Banks,' and the statutory phrase 'inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office.' source-1.html.gz (CBS News): CONFIRMS the overruling of the 1935 for-cause precedent, the majority quote 'Subordinates who exercise the President's power are subject to removal by him,' the Sotomayor quote 'Dozens of independent commissions are now likely to become purely executive agencies,' the FERC/NRC/NLRB list and 'more than two dozen' framing, and the Fed carve-out quote 'does not implicate the constitutionality of the Fed's removal restrictions.' source-2.html.gz (IAPP): CONFIRMS the quote 'The President must have the assistance of officers he can trust,' Slaughter's reaction quoting a 'unanimous, 91-year-old precedent,' and the privacy/AI enforcement framing. Every one of the ~12 direct quotes appears verbatim in the correctly attributed snapshot.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics trace to a cited source: case name Trump v. Slaughter and docket No. 25-332 (SCOTUSblog), decision date June 29 2026 (SCOTUSblog), 6-3 vote (SCOTUSblog; CBS states '6 to 3'), 1935 Humphrey's Executor and 91-year span (all three), and the affected-agency list (CBS). No hallucinations detected. The article's '91 years old' matches the source '91-year-old precedent' (1935 to 2026). editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout. The article reports the ruling factually without editorializing or taking a political side. It gives the majority's reasoning and the dissent's objection comparable weight and direct-quote representation, and frames the tech consequences ('may pursue those cases more aggressively or drop them, depending on the priorities of the sitting President') as conditional rather than advocacy. No loaded language, no sensationalism, no AI self-reference.
